source.text: Τοὺς δὲ κατακοπτομένους καὶ μακρὰν ῥιπτομένους ἀπὸ τοῦ πύργου θέλεις γνῶναι; οὗτοί εἰσιν οἱ υἱοὶ τῆς ἀνομίας· ἐπίστευσαν δὲ ἐν ὑποκρίσει, καὶ πᾶσα πονηρία οὐκ ἀπέστη ἀπʼ αὐτῶν· διὰ τοῦτο οὐκ ἔχουσιν σωτηρίαν, ὅτι οὐκ εἰσὶν εὔχρηστοι εἰς οἰκοδομὴν διὰ τὰς πονηρίας αὐτῶν. διὰ 20—2 τοῦτο συνεκόπησαν καὶ πόρρω ἀπερίφησαν διὰ τὴν ὀργὴν τοῦ Κυρίου, ὅτι παρώργισαν αὐτόν. 2. τοὺς δὲ ἑτέρους οὓς ἑώρακας πολλοὺς κειμένους, μὴ ὑπάγοντας εἰς τὴν οἰκοδομήν, οὗτοι οἱ μὲν ἐψωριακότες εἰσίν, οἱ ἐγνωκότες τὴν ἀλήθειαν, μὴ ἐπιμείναντες δὲ ἐν αὐτῇ μηδὲ κολλώμενοι τοῖς ἁγίοις· διὰ τοῦτο ἄχρηστοί εἰσιν. 3. Οἱ δὲ τὰς σχισμὰς ἔχοντες τίνες εἰσίν; Οὗτοί εἰσιν οἱ κατ᾿ ἀλλήλων ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ἔχοντες καὶ μὴ εἰρηνεύοντες ἐν ἑαυτοῖς, ἀλλὰ πρόσωπον εἰρήνης ἔχοντες, ὅταν δὲ ἀπ᾿ ἀλλήλων ἀποχωρήσωσιν, αἱ πονηρίαι αὐτῶν ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ἐμμένουσιν. αὗται οὖν αἱ σχισμαί εἰσιν ἃς ἔχουσιν οἱ λίθοι. 4. οἱ δὲ κεκολοβωμένοι, οὗτοί εἰσιν πεπιστευκότες μὲν καὶ τὸ πλεῖον μέρος ἔχοντες ἐν τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ, τινὰ δὲ μέρη ἔχουσιν τῆς ἀνομίας· διὰ τοῦτο κολοβοὶ καὶ οὐχ ὁλοτελεῖς εἰσίν. 5. Οἱ δὲ λευκοὶ καὶ στρογγύλοι καὶ μὴ ἁρμόζοντες εἰς τὴν οἰκοδομὴν τίνες εἰσίν, κυρία; ἀποκριθεῖσά μοι λέγει· Ἕως πότε μωρὸς εἶ καὶ ἀσύνετος, καὶ πάντα ἐπερωτᾷς καὶ οὐδὲν νοεῖς; οὗτοί εἰσιν ἔχοντες μὲν πίστιν, ἔχοντες δὲ καὶ πλοῦτον τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου. ὅταν γένηται θλῖψις, διὰ τὸν πλοῦτον αὐτῶν καὶ διὰ τὰς πραγματείας ἀπαρνοῦνται τὸν Κύριον αὐτῶν. 6. καὶ ἀποκριθεὶς αὐτῇ λέγω· Κυρία, πότε οὖν εὔχρηστοι ἔσονται εἰς τὴν οἰκοδομήν; Ὅταν, φησίν, περικοπῇ αὐτῶν ὁ πλοῦτος ὁ ψυχαγωγῶν αὐτούς, τότε εὔχρηστοι ἔσονται τῷ Θεῷ. ὥσπερ γὰρ ὁ λίθος ὁ στρογγύλος ἐὰν μὴ περικοπῇ καὶ ἀποβάλῃ ἐξ αὐτοῦ τι, οὐ δύναται τετράγωνος γενέσθαι, οὕτω καὶ οἱ πλουτοῦντες ἐν τούτῳ τῷ αἰῶνι, ἐὰν μὴ περικοπῇ αὐτῶν ὁ πλοῦτος, οὐ δύνανται τῷ Κυρίῳ εὔχρηστοι γενέσθαι. 7. ἀπὸ [δὲ] σεαυτοῦ πρῶτον γνῶθι· ὅτε ἐπλούτεις, ἄχρηστος ἦς· νῦν δὲ εὔχρηστος εἶ καὶ ὠφέλιμος τῇ ζωῇ. εὔχρηστοι γίνεσθε τῷ Θεῷ· καὶ γὰρ σὺ αὐτὸς χρᾶσαι ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν λίθων.

translation.text:
“Do you want to know about those who are being cut down and hurled far from the tower? These are the sons of lawlessness[a]; they believed in hypocrisy, and no wickedness departed from them. For this reason they have no salvation, because they are not serviceable for the building on account of their wicked deeds. Therefore they were cut away and flung far off because of the anger of the Lord, because they provoked him.

2. “And the others you saw—many lying there, not going into the building—these are the scabbed ones: they came to know the truth, but did not remain in it, nor did they cling to the holy ones; therefore they are useless.

3. “And those that have cracks—who are they? These are the ones who harbor things against one another in their hearts and are not at peace among themselves, but put on a face of peace; yet when they depart from one another, their evils remain in their hearts. These, then, are the cracks that the stones have.

4. “And the ones cut short—these are those who have believed and have the greater part in righteousness, but have certain parts of lawlessness. For this reason they are truncated and not whole.

5. “And the white and round ones that do not fit into the building—who are they, Lady?” She answered me, saying, “How long will you be foolish and without understanding, asking about everything and understanding nothing? These are those who have faith, but also have the wealth of this age. When affliction comes, because of their wealth and their business dealings they deny their Lord.”

6. And I answered her, “Lady, when then will they become fit for the building?” She said, “When their wealth—which captivates their souls—has been cut back, then they will be useful to God. For just as a round stone, unless it is trimmed and sheds something from itself, cannot become square, so also those who are rich in this age, unless their wealth is cut back, cannot become useful to the Lord.

7. “Learn first from yourself: when you were rich, you were useless; but now you are useful and beneficial for life. Become useful to God[b][c][d][e][f][g][h]; for you yourself also are used from the same stones.”

footnotes.text: Semitic idiom meaning people characterized by lawlessness; retained literally to preserve tone.
Greek ἐψωριακότες derives from ψώρα ‘scab, itch.’ Alternatives: ‘scabby,’ ‘mange-covered.’ ‘Leprous’ is not accurate here.
Greek σχίσματα can also mean ‘divisions’ or ‘schisms.’ ‘Cracks’ fits the stone metaphor; the ecclesial sense is acknowledged here.
ψυχαγωγῶν often means to charm or entertain; the phrase highlights the seductive pull of wealth.
Literally ‘four‑cornered’ (τετράγωνος), the standard shape for stones that fit securely in ancient masonry.
Some witnesses include δὲ (‘and/but’) after ἀπὸ: ‘And learn first from yourself.’ The sense is unchanged.

Greek χρᾶσαι ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν λίθων is syntactically awkward. Taken deponently: ‘you make use of…’; some interpret it passively, ‘you are also used from the same stones,’ i.e., selected as a stone for the building.
Or 'Become useful to God; for even you yourself make use of the same stones.'.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Maintains the violent image of stones being cut away, consistent with the tower-building metaphor.
Conveys force (not a gentle placing) and pairs well with ‘cut down’ to intensify the judgment image.
Preserves Semitic idiom ‘sons of …’ and the moral characterization without smoothing into generic ‘lawless people.’
Retains explicit mention of ‘hypocrisy’ rather than paraphrasing; this keeps Hermas’s moral register sharp.
Echoes the somewhat formal, concrete phrasing of the Greek, preserving the moral category ‘wickedness.’
‘Salvation’ is the established soteriological term; alternatives would understate the gravity in this context.
Keeps the construction metaphor explicit (‘building’) and uses ‘serviceable’ to match the utilitarian imagery of stones.
In the stone-building context, ‘cut away’ fits well and ties to later ‘trimming’ language.
Preserves both the rejection (‘cast off’) and the distance (‘far’), intensifying the exclusion image.
‘Anger’ conveys divine displeasure without importing later technical nuances of ‘wrath’; aligns with Cartha’s default for Kyrios as ‘Lord.’
ψώρα denotes scab/itch; ‘scabbed’ retains the concrete, unflattering image without medical anachronism (‘leprous’).
‘Remain’ is a direct, transparent rendering that preserves the simple aspect of staying in the truth.

alternatives: attach themselves to the holy ones
lexical_decisions.rationale: ‘Cling’ mirrors the metaphor of adhesion and community bond; ‘holy ones’ retains the literal phrase instead of ecclesiastical ‘saints.’
Within the stone imagery, ‘cracks’ is the most concrete; a footnote notes the ecclesial sense ‘divisions/schisms.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: harbor things against one another in their hearts
alternatives: having things against each other in their hearts
lexical_decisions.rationale: ‘Harbor’ captures an ongoing inner posture consistent with the allegory’s interior focus.
Retains the vivid idiom (face/mask), highlighting duplicity.
In the stone context, ‘cut short/truncated’ conveys incompleteness without medical connotations.
Simple, idiomatic opposite to ‘truncated’; matches the moral picture of integrity.
Direct description preserves the visual of clean, smooth stones that do not interlock.
‘Fit’ is the standard building term for stones that interlock in construction.
Retains the temporal contrast (‘this age’) central to Hermas’s moral economy.
‘Affliction’ is natural English and matches the context of testing; ‘tribulation’ is heavier but more technical.
Conveys mercantile/transactional nuance without archaic ‘traffickings.’
Echoes the stone-cutting metaphor and communicates reduction without suggesting total renunciation.
ψυχαγωγέω in classical usage means to lead/captivate the soul, often with entertainment; ‘captivates’ carries the pull/attraction idea.
‘Square’ is idiomatic; footnote notes literal ‘four-cornered,’ an ancient building ideal.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who are rich in this age
alternatives: those who prosper in this age
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps verbal aspect of ongoing wealth and the temporal frame.
Simple, direct antonyms that the passage repeatedly contrasts; fits the tool-like imagery.
‘Beneficial’ captures moral/spiritual advantage without commercial overtones.

lexical_decisions.chosen: make use of the same stones
alternatives: are also used from the same stones
lexical_decisions.rationale: χράομαι is middle deponent ‘to use’; prepositional ἐκ indicates source/selection. The phrasing preserves the Greek structure while a footnote notes the alternative passive-like sense some see in context.

theological_decisions.rationale: Preserves the literal communal identity without importing later ecclesiastical coloration; aligns with Cartha’s aim to keep early-church texture concrete.

theological_decisions.issue: σχίσματα in a stone allegory vs. ecclesial schism
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Render as ‘cracks’ in the main text.
theological_decisions.rationale: In this immediate context, the visual of cracked stones is primary; a footnote preserves awareness of the term’s later ecclesial sense to avoid over-reading church-order polemic here.
Follows project default for Kyrios to render ‘Lord,’ reflecting covenantal usage without over-specific christological import within Hermas’s visionary context.
Here πίστις is a possessed quality (‘having faith’) alongside wealth; ‘faith’ is the clear, established sense.

review_passes.summary: The draft is generally excellent and captures Hermas's tone well. However, there are a few minor issues: a literal rendering of a negative idiom that creates awkward English, an active participle translated as passive, the insertion of rhetorical questions where the Greek has statements, and some mismatched quotation marks across the dialogue in verses 5–7.
issues_found: In verse 1, 'every wickedness did not depart' is a literal rendering of the Greek/Semitic idiom (πᾶσα ... οὐκ) which means 'no wickedness departed.' The literal English is awkward and could be misread as 'not every wickedness departed.'
In verse 2, 'not being brought' translates the active/intransitive participle ὑπάγοντας as passive. It should be 'not going,' consistent with its translation in the previous section.
In verses 2 and 4, the draft inserts rhetorical questions ('who are these?', 'who are they?') to match the pattern of other verses, but the Greek explicitly uses statements here (οὗτοι ... εἰσίν).
In verses 5–7, quotation marks are mismatched and unclosed, confusing the boundaries of the dialogue.

translation.text: “Do you want to know about those who are being cut down and thrown far from the tower? These are the sons of lawlessness; they believed in hypocrisy, and no wickedness departed from them. For this reason they have no salvation, because they are not fit for the building on account of their wicked deeds. Therefore they were cut down and thrown far away because of the anger of the Lord, because they provoked him.

spob_revision_history.previous_text: 5. I asked, “Lady, who are the white, round stones that do not fit into the building?” She replied, “How long will you remain foolish and fail to understand? You ask about everything, yet understand nothing. These stones are people who have faith but are also rich in this world. When suffering comes, they deny their Lord because they are concerned about their wealth and business.”
spob_revision_history.review_summary: The draft usefully identifies the vision objects as stones and explains that they represent people, making the symbolic scene accessible without adding doctrine. “Rich in this world” adequately clarifies “the wealth of this age.” Revise the final causal clause, however: “concerned about” weakens the passage’s direct claim that wealth and business dealings lead to denial under suffering.

base_translation.text: 6. And I answered her, “Lady, when then will they become fit for the building?” She said, “When their wealth that ensnares them has been cut away, then they will be useful to God. For just as a round stone, unless it is cut and casts off something from itself, cannot become square, so also those who are rich in this age, unless their wealth is cut away, cannot become useful to the Lord.

translation.text: 6. I asked her, “Lady, when will they be ready to be used in the building?” She answered, “They will be useful to God when the wealth that traps them has been cut away. A round stone cannot be made square unless it is cut and some of it is removed. In the same way, the rich people of this age cannot be useful to the Lord unless their wealth is cut away.”

simplification_decisions.reasoning_layer_used: POB text and immediate stone-building context
simplification_decisions.rationale: The new wording makes their intended use clear without explaining away the image.

simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: the wealth that traps them
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: Their wealth holds them back from being useful to God.
simplification_decisions.rationale: “Traps” expresses the force of “ensnares” in common English.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: unless it is cut and casts off something from itself
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: unless it is cut and some of it is removed
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: Part of the round stone must be cut away so it can become square.

risk_flags.risk: Readers may take “wealth is cut away” as a complete explanation of how the rich are changed.
risk_flags.mitigation: The draft preserves the POB’s concrete image without adding an unsupported interpretation.

base_translation.text: 7. “Learn first from yourself: when you were rich, you were useless; but now you are useful and beneficial for life. Become useful to God; for you yourself also are used from the same stones.”

translation.text: 7. “First, learn from your own experience. When you were rich, you were useless. But now you are useful in ways that benefit life. Make yourself useful to God, because you too are being put to use with these same stones.[a]”

footnotes.text: The wording links the hearer with the stones but does not clearly state the exact relationship.

simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: First, learn from your own experience
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The hearer is to recognize the lesson by reflecting on his own changed condition.
simplification_decisions.rationale: The reflexive expression is recast in natural English without changing its point.

simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: useful in ways that benefit life
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: His present usefulness benefits life, without specifying who receives that benefit.
simplification_decisions.rationale: This clarifies the abstract phrase without claiming that he brings life to others.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: you yourself also are used from the same stones
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: you too are being put to use with these same stones
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The hearer is connected with the same stone image and is also put to use.
simplification_decisions.reasoning_layer_used: POB translation, source-language image, and grounding review
simplification_decisions.rationale: The stone image remains while the difficult relationship is left open.

risk_flags.risk: “Benefit life” remains broad because the POB does not identify a particular recipient or kind of benefit.
risk_flags.mitigation: The draft avoids adding “others” or saying that the hearer brings life.

risk_flags.risk: The exact relationship between the hearer and the stones is grammatically uncertain.
risk_flags.mitigation: The main text uses the broad link “with,” and the footnote preserves the uncertainty.

spob_revision_history.previous_text: 7. “First, learn from your own experience. When you were rich, you were useless. But now you are useful and help bring life to others. Make yourself useful to God, because you too are being used as one of these stones.”
spob_revision_history.review_summary: The opening clarification is natural and warranted by the reflexive wording and the before-and-after contrast. The draft is clearer overall, but its rendering of “beneficial for life” adds an unestablished claim that the hearer helps bring life to other people. It also over-resolves the acknowledged difficulty of the stone clause. The replacement preserves the legitimate clarity gain while retaining the source/POB scope and ambiguity.
